prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Not, Angels, They

outputs.L1:
Not that I understand these things. Angels don't walk toward the ship in this old engraving, where the moon throws a river of light—though surely angels could walk the ocean, if they wished to walk. They don't. They hover. Considerable space lies between them and what shines like waves. This can't be a matter of choice, neither for the angels nor for the engraver, who was, in fact, Gustave Doré, recovering from the ancient mariner Coleridge left behind, burdened by guilt and regret and the weight of an albatross.

Not much weight, admittedly, but they are large birds—four feet across, counting the wind and rain that travel with them. Doré waking in a room that held no wings at all. I imagine a stirring, something in the black expanse he hoped to razor into the copper plate—no, a graver, not a razor at all.

Beauty does terrify—a bare nothing, and yet it stops you. As with angels. Abrupt. Still, cutting their flight into metal takes time. His hands stiff, Doré working under deadline, no doubt, like the rest of us, endlessly and after the fact, doing what we do, and do, until it is no longer what we do.

Nevertheless, angels. Why did they keep coming, one by one, radiant against the dark of a mind paused on this most desolate given: water at night. That it floods a future not even present in the picture.
outputs.L2:
It's not as though I grasp any of this. In the old print, celestial beings don't stride toward the vessel where moonlight pours down like flowing water—showing how they might cross the sea if walking were their intent. Instead they float, suspended, with considerable distance separating them from the glimmering swells below. This separation wasn't a decision either they or their creator made freely—that creator being Gustave Doré, recovering from his encounter with Coleridge's mariner, that figure left behind carrying shame, sorrow, and the burden of a dead bird. Not such a heavy weight really, though these creatures span four feet when you factor in their wingspan through wind and storm.

Doré emerged from sleep into a space empty of any actual wings. Perhaps something stirred within the darkness he intended to carve into copper—using an engraving tool, not a blade as I first said.

Genuine beauty stops you cold, creates a kind of absence. This is what angels do: they halt movement entirely. Yet transferring their suspended flight onto metal required patience and time. His fingers grew rigid, no doubt racing against some publisher's timeline, much like the rest of us continue our labor, repeating actions until those actions no longer define us.

And still, the angels persisted—emerging one after another, each luminous point within a consciousness that had gone quiet before this bleakest of truths: the ocean at midnight. How it overflows into some future moment that exists nowhere within the frame itself.
outputs.L3:
# On Angels Suspended Above the Water: A Reading of Doré's Vision

The poem takes as its subject one of Gustave Doré's most haunting engravings—an illustration created for Samuel Taylor Coleridge's "The Rime of the Ancient Mariner." In this image, celestial beings hover above a vast, moonlit expanse of ocean, their forms caught between the ethereal and the tangible. The poem does not merely describe this scene but meditates upon it, using Doré's visual composition as a lens through which to explore questions of creation, labor, and transcendence. The moonlight, rendered through Doré's masterful use of light and shadow, becomes not simply a source of illumination but an active participant in the scene, silvering the waves and casting the angels in a spectral glow that seems to emanate from within the image itself rather than from any single source of light.

Central to the poem's contemplation is the peculiar positioning of these angelic figures: they do not walk upon the water, nor do they touch its surface in any conventional sense. Instead, they hover—suspended in a liminal space above the shimmering waves, maintaining a deliberate and unbridgeable distance from the ocean below. The poem suggests this separation serves a dual purpose. On one hand, it speaks to the fundamental nature of angels themselves—beings who exist outside the physical laws that govern mortal creatures, for whom contact with earthly elements like water would be almost a category error, a violation of their essential otherness. On the other hand, this hovering quality reflects Doré's own artistic sensibility, his instinct to preserve a sense of mystery and remove by refusing to let the sacred and the earthly fully touch. The distance, then, becomes both theological statement and aesthetic choice, each reinforcing the other.

The poem draws a striking and deliberate contrast between the sublime nature of the angels themselves and the mundane, physical reality of their creation. These beings, meant to evoke terror and beauty in equal measure—vast, luminous, almost incomprehensible in their power—exist paradoxically as the product of an intensely tedious and mechanical process. Doré would have carved these figures into a copper plate using a graver, a tool requiring steady hands, immense patience, and countless small, careful strokes. The poem lingers on this incongruity: how something meant to represent the infinite and the divine emerges from such finite, repetitive human labor. Each line that suggests the sweep of an angel's wing or the fall of celestial light required physical exertion, minute calculation, and the acceptance of the medium's unforgiving nature—for copper does not forgive mistakes easily, and the graver's mark, once made, resists easy correction.

This tension between the transcendent subject matter and the grinding reality of its production leads the poem toward a broader meditation on Doré's working conditions and, by extension, the human condition more generally. The poem imagines Doré laboring under the pressure of deadlines, his artistic vision constrained and shaped by the practical demands of publication schedules, patron expectations, and the sheer physical toll of engraving work. This portrait of the artist becomes emblematic of something larger: the way human beings persist in their labor, often mechanically and without clear reprieve, until either the purpose behind that labor dissolves or transforms into something else entirely. There is an implicit commentary here on how creative work—even work depicting the sublime and the eternal—remains tethered to the temporal, the deadline-driven, the exhausting repetition of daily toil.

The poem concludes not with resolution but with a persistent, unanswered question: why do angels continue to appear, again and again, within the artist's imaginative landscape? This inquiry is left deliberately open, unresolved, as the poem instead turns its attention to the image's atmosphere—a desolate, timeless vision of water at night that seems to extend infinitely beyond the literal borders of the engraving itself. The ocean depicted becomes more than a setting; it transforms into a kind of eternal presence, suggesting that the angels' appearance is inextricably linked to this vast, dark, and ancient body of water. The poem closes by allowing this image to linger unresolved, suggesting that some questions about creative inspiration, spiritual presence, and artistic obsession resist tidy answers, existing instead in the same suspended, hovering state as the angels themselves—present, undeniable, yet perpetually out of reach.
outputs.L4:
**Hovering**
*after Gustave Doré's illustration for "The Rime of the Ancient Mariner"*

Consider the angels first—how they refuse
the sea's insistence on a surface,
how they simply will not walk,
will not so much as dip a sandaled toe
into that engraved and endless swell.
They hover instead, inexplicably lit
from some source outside the frame,
robes gathered like held breath,
wings a suggestion rather than a mechanism.

Doré must have known this was impossible.
Not the theology—he'd drawn worse miracles—
but the practical matter of rendering weightlessness
in a medium that is nothing but weight:
copper, acid, the burin's patient bite,
each line a small, irreversible decision
made by a hand that had perhaps not slept,
a hand racing some publisher's calendar,
some deadline circled in another man's ledger
while the mariner's ship sailed on regardless,
becalmed in its argument with God.

Think of the labor in that lightness.
Think of him hunched over the plate for hours,
scratching into the metal's cold face
the illusion of things that need not scratch
for purchase anywhere, that hover
by some logic he could gesture toward
but never quite explain—the way
his own hand could not fly, could not hover,
could only press and press and press
until the burin's groove filled up with black,
with the printer's ink that would become,
on paper, on someone's reading table,
the strange cold light these angels stand in.

This is the trouble with transcendence:
it will not hold still to be copied.
It asks the human hand to reproduce
what the human hand cannot itself perform,
and so there is something terrible
in the angels' calm, something that undoes
the comfort we expect from holy figures—
not gentleness, but a vertigo,
the sense that beauty, when it is real,
refuses to explain its own suspension,
refuses to say how it is done,
leaving us to stare at the engraved sea
and feel the floor of our understanding
drop away beneath us like a deck
in a ship gone terribly still.

And after the poem closes, after
the mariner tells his tale to the wedding guest
who leaves "a sadder and a wiser man,"
the angels do not leave. They hover still,
in that separate country the engraving keeps,
beyond the last line, beyond the closing plate,
beyond whatever hour Doré finally
set down his tools and rubbed his eyes
and looked, perhaps, at his own trembling hands—
and the desolation does not stay bound there either.
It leaks out past the border of the print,
into whatever room you're standing in
right now, holding the book, uncertain
of the morning that will follow this one,
uncertain if the light you're waiting for
will hover, too, just out of reach,
inexplicable, and terrible, and true.
outputs.L5:
# Not Angels, They

They walk among us with tired eyes,
carrying groceries up narrow stairs,
sitting beside strangers in waiting rooms,
offering the last seat on a crowded train.

Not angels, they.

No wings unfold from their shoulders,
no halos crown their unwashed hair.
They stumble, they forget, they fail—
and still they show up, again and again.

We call them angels sometimes,
when their kindness catches us off guard,
when a stranger's small mercy
feels too large for this ordinary world.

But that name does them a disservice.
It lifts them out of reach,
places their goodness in some distant realm
where struggle doesn't touch,
where doubt has no foothold,
where choice was never required.

They are not angels.

They are the tired nurse at 3 a.m.
who still speaks softly.
They are the neighbor who shovels
one more driveway than his own.
They are the ones who chose,
in some small and unremarkable moment,
to be gentle when cruelty would have been easier.

This is what makes it matter—
not that they were born to shine,
but that they chose to, anyway,
in a world that gave them every reason not to.

Not angels.
Just people.
Which is harder,
and so much more remarkable.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse poem inspired by Gustave Doré’s engravings for Coleridge’s "The Rime of the Ancient Mariner," focusing on the image of angels above the ship.
counterfactuals.output:
**Seraphim Over the Becalmed**

Doré carved the light before he carved the dark—
see how the burin bites deeper where the wings begin,
each feather a wound opened in the paper's white flesh,
radiating outward like the halo
around a struck match in a coal mine.

The ship is a black tooth in a mouth of glass.
Below: the corpse-crew, still lashed to their ropes,
mouths open in the shape of prayers
they will never finish speaking.
Above: this crowd of burning men,
if men is the word for such geometry of light—

they hover the way smoke hovers
before it decides which way the wind wants it,
robes like poured wax, wings like the undersides
of storm clouds struck by lightning from within.

I have stared at this plate so long
the ink has become a kind of weather.
Notice how Doré never gives them faces—
only the suggestion of faces,
the way you'd draw the sun
if you were forbidden to look at it,
a blank where the eyes should burn.

They do not reach down.
They do not lift the dead sailors' arms
or close their staring eyes.
They only stand in the rigging like a second sky,
a ceiling of grace the ship did not ask for
and cannot refuse.

This is the cruelty and the mercy of the engraving—
that redemption looks like this:
distant, radiant, utterly still,
a crowd of witnesses
who will not save you
but will not look away either.

The mariner below, still breathing, still guilty,
squints up into that terrible brightness
the way you'd squint into your own conscience
grown suddenly, unbearably visible—

and the sea holds the ship in its black palm,
and the angels hold their light like a secret,
and Doré's hand, two hundred years gone,
still holds the burin steady,
still cuts the white so carefully
into the shape of what we cannot earn.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a contemplative poem about angels that don't quite touch the world, blending imagery of moonlight, water, and an old illustrator working under deadline?
counterfactuals.output:
**Undrawn**

He draws them at the hour the moon
leans its whole weight against the window,
a thumbprint of silver smudging the glass,
while the deadline waits like a held breath
beside the coffee gone cold on the table.

Each angel he renders hovers
an inch above the page—
never landing, never quite
sinking into the paper's grain,
as though graphite were a river
too swift to wade,
too deep for holy feet.

He has always drawn them this way:
wings caught mid-fold, like moonlight
caught on water—
not held, only visiting,
a coin of light that slides
and will not settle.

Sixty years of ink and deadlines,
and still he cannot make them land.
Perhaps this is not failure
but faithfulness—
some things are only true
in the space just before touching,
the breath before the foot finds floor,
the ripple before the stone.

He remembers a lake once, at night,
how the moon lay on it whole
yet broke apart if he reached his hand in,
how the water kept the light
by never quite keeping it.

So he leaves an inch of white
beneath each pair of feet he draws—
not laziness, not an unfinished thing,
but the only accurate distance
between what glows
and what it glows upon.

The morning courier will come too soon.
He will hand over the pages
still faintly warm from the lamp,
each angel suspended, unlanded,
like moonlight that has agreed
to almost become water,
like water that has agreed
to almost hold the sky—

and somewhere in that almost,
he thinks, is where the sacred
has always chosen to live.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a modern poem in a stream-of-consciousness style that reflects on a famous illustration of the Ancient Mariner, mixing philosophical musing with historical detail about the artist.
counterfactuals.output:
**Looking at Doré's Mariner, 1876**

Cross-hatched dark like the inside of an eye closing—
             *and I think: Gustave was only forty when this came out,*
             a boy-wonder from Strasbourg who never stopped drawing,
             ten thousand lines a day some said, hand cramped
             into the shape of prayer or curse, who knows which—

the ship tilts on the page the way guilt tilts a life,
that impossible angle where the horizon 
refuses to hold still, refuses to be horizon at all—

*was the albatross ever really there*
or only the shape guilt makes when it needs
a body to hang around a throat—

Doré never left Paris for the sea, did he,
never salted his boots on any deck,
just sat in that apartment on rue Saint-Dominique
imagining ice that groaned like something human,
imagining men gone the color of parchment,
their eyes two flat coins the ferryman forgot to take—

              this is what illustration does—
              it fixes suffering into a single instant
              the way memory does, unfair, unchanging,
              the moment before the moment after
              collapsed into one held breath of steel-cut line—

I keep looking at the hand that made this hand
that made the wedding guest turn his face away—
the French thought Doré too much, too dark, too German
in his excess, while the English loved him,
loved the way he understood damnation
as something with weather in it, something wet—

*and isn't that the trick of guilt too—
it always comes with weather,
comes with cold that isn't really cold
but something the soul invented
to give its shame a temperature—*

He died at fifty-one, still working,
some story about a heart that simply
stopped keeping time, the way a metronome
stops and the music you were playing
becomes just noise, just arms moving
through air that no longer answers back—

I think the Mariner is still out there
in the white space between the lines
Doré didn't draw, still telling it,
still needing someone to stop, to listen,
to be stoppered by the story
the way the wedding guest was stoppered,

              *because isn't that all any of us want—
              not forgiveness exactly, not really,*
              *but a witness, someone to hold the shape
              of what happened long enough
              that it becomes bearable to have happened at all—*

the engraving does that, doesn't it,
holds the drowning open forever,
holds the guilt of one dead bird
suspended above black water
that never finishes being black—

Doré's ghost still bent over his table,
still scratching at the plate,
still trying to get the ice to sound
the way it sounds in nightmares—
and mine, still trying to say
what this old story keeps telling me
about the weight we carry
because we killed something
that only wanted to follow the ship home.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a lyric poem that explores themes of guilt, beauty, and creative labor, using the visual motif of angels hovering over a nighttime sea as inspired by classic literary illustration.
counterfactuals.output:
# Night Work

The angels come at the hour when guilt
loosens its collar, when the sea
forgets which sins it swallowed whole
and lies there, silver, unconfessed.

I have made this scene before—
in ink, in wax, in the small hours
when the hand knows more than the mind allows,
tracing wings from memory of no wings,
feathers that are really just
the way light refuses to sit still on water.

They hover, these messengers, not touching down,
as if the sea were too finished a thing,
too much already art, and they
mere commentary, mere glosses
in the margin of something vast and done.

This is the trouble with beauty—
it asks to be witnessed
and witnessing is its own small theft.
I take the scene and make it mine.
I press it into paper, into form,
and something dies to become permanent.

The angels do not blame me for this.
They have their own guilt, hovering
between the human and the unbearable,
between the given world and the one
they're tasked to bless but cannot enter.

Look how the water holds their reflection
without holding them.
Look how the labor of making
is always this: to reach for radiance
and come back with your hands
full of something merely luminous,
merely true, merely the sea at night
doing what it does
whether or not the angels come,
whether or not I stay up
trying to net the unrepeatable
in lines that will, tomorrow,
look like any other lines—

marks a hand once made
reaching toward what hovered,
what shone,
what would not stay to be forgiven.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
